articles.title: I can build the product with AI. Getting the first users is harder.
articles.description: What building Brainy and MoneyBrain taught me about finding early users beyond my LinkedIn network, and what I want to try next.
articles.body_html:
With Brainy and MoneyBrain, getting the first users and growing monthly recurring revenue has been harder than building the software.

At the beginning, I used my circles on LinkedIn. It gave me somewhere to start talking about the products. Expanding beyond that network has been difficult, especially without a large budget.

That is where I want to pick up from my previous post about building products with AI. In that post, I described how I move from a brainstorm to requirements, GitHub issues, implementation, and a reviewed pull request. I can give the implementation work a scope and check the result against it.

Finding users leaves me with questions I am still working through: where to reach people who need the product, and why they would try it, return, and eventually pay.

My network gave me a place to start

Talking about Brainy and MoneyBrain on LinkedIn was a reasonable first step. I already had people I could reach there, rather than starting with an empty account and hoping someone would find a product announcement.

But a professional network is a particular audience. Someone can be interested in how I build software without needing either product. A post about my AI workflow and a post explaining why someone should use an application ask for different kinds of attention.

More visibility for me would be useful, but I also need to understand which people have the problem the product addresses. Otherwise, I could spend more time promoting it and still learn very little about demand.

A screenshot of a SaaS advice post brought this back into focus. It covered familiar recommendations: promote the product, talk to users, keep the first version small, use it yourself, and pay attention to people who leave.

Reading those points alongside my experience, I kept returning to the difficulty of reaching the next group of people without a large budget.

The post puts most of the work after launch into marketing. I would not assign a fixed percentage to it, but I agree with the underlying reminder: launching leaves a substantial amount of work ahead. For my current goal of finding users, time spent explaining the product and following up with people deserves a place in the schedule alongside implementation. Another completed issue does not tell me whether anyone new understood the offer.

Reaching outside my LinkedIn circles

The encouragement to promote the product openly is useful. Staying entirely within my familiar LinkedIn circles would leave the same audience boundary in place. I need to be willing to explain what I have built somewhere people do not already know me, and to hear that it may not be relevant to them.

I could make a long list of places to post. Each one would take time to understand, participate in, and follow up on. I would also have to decide what to say there, because a product announcement that makes sense to my LinkedIn contacts may mean very little to a stranger.

For Brainy and MoneyBrain, I would rather make the next attempt narrow enough to learn from. Pick one product, one specific problem, and one place where people already discuss that problem. Then explain or demonstrate the part of the product that addresses it.

I also need to make that choice separately for each product. The fact that I built both does not mean the same people need both, or that the same explanation will persuade them. Putting their names into one announcement is convenient for me; a potential user needs a reason to care about the particular application in front of them.

I could examine the result: did people recognize the problem, ask how the product handles their situation, or try it?

If the only response is interest in the technology behind it, that would tell me something too. I might have reached other builders, or explained the implementation more clearly than the reason to use the product.

I feel the budget constraint, but I do not want to turn that into a conclusion that growth requires a large advertising spend. I have not established that. Before spending more, I want a clearer idea of whom I am trying to reach and what I can show them.

A useful next asset could be a short walkthrough of one task, using demonstration data and showing the result. I could use it in a relevant conversation, give the landing page something concrete to show, and learn which part needs more explanation. A tutorial answering a question prospective users already ask could also become something they can find or share later. These would give me more to work with than repeatedly announcing that the product exists.

A community, a search-focused article, or a collaboration needs to earn the time I put into it. A channel with no advertising bill still costs time. Participating well in a community means reading the discussions, respecting its rules, and contributing something useful before expecting attention for my application.

The alternative is often something people already do

Before writing that walkthrough, I need to understand what the person would replace. They might already have a tool, a document, or a routine that handles the task adequately. Moving to my product could mean learning another interface and spending time setting it up before they see a benefit.

My own move from Notion to Brainy is a useful example of an existing workflow being involved. It gives me a case to examine, but another person's reasons to change could be different. I need to ask which part of their current approach is frustrating enough to justify the effort of switching.

That should shape the product description. Explaining the task someone can complete gives them a way to judge the offer. Describing my AI-assisted development process tells them how I made it. I enjoy talking about that process, and it belongs in the previous post, but it may have little bearing on a person's decision to use Brainy or MoneyBrain.

Even the comparison with competitors needs this context. A competing subscription price tells me one thing about the market; a person's current workaround tells me what I would have to improve. If their approach is already good enough, I need to understand that answer instead of assuming another feature will persuade them.

The first visit needs somewhere useful to go

Someone outside my network needs to understand the product without knowing my background. That makes the advice about the landing page and sign-up process more relevant.

A useful check would be to ask someone unfamiliar with the project to look at the page and explain what they think it does. Then ask them to attempt its main task. I would want to see where they hesitate before adding another feature to the backlog.

That is how I read the advice to make a landing page clean, fast, and convincing. Keep the page focused, check how it loads on a phone, and show a concrete use of the product. A polished layout still needs to help that unfamiliar visitor decide whether to try it.

Google login might remove a step for some people. It cannot explain an unclear product promise, and I would not treat it as an automatic requirement for every audience. The question I want to investigate is where a prospective user gets stuck between understanding the offer and experiencing something useful.

Using my own product regularly gives me a way to notice friction in ordinary tasks. In my earlier post about moving to European digital services, I described replacing Notion with Brainy. That is a useful starting point for testing a real workflow. But I know the product's intended behavior and can navigate around something that another person would find confusing. My familiarity is a reason to get an outside view, especially when I am asking that person to trust a new product.

Keeping the minimum viable product small belongs in this discussion too. I want enough functionality to let someone complete the task that brought them there. Adding features before understanding that task could make both the explanation and the first visit more complicated.

The screenshot names MoSCoW as a way to keep that scope under control: Must Have, Should Have, Could Have, and Won't Have this time. The Agile Business Consortium explains those priorities. For a first release, I would ask whether leaving a feature out prevents the intended user from completing the core task. If it does not, I need a good reason to put it ahead of learning from users.

For the first users, I would also consider helping them through that task personally. Paul Graham's essay on doing things that don't scale argues for recruiting early users manually and paying close attention to their experience. I can see a practical application here: offer a short walkthrough, watch where the person needs help, and use that observation to improve the next attempt.

If I have to explain the same step to everyone, that gives me something specific to investigate in the interface or instructions. If each person wants a completely different outcome, I need to revisit the audience and scope. Automating the welcome messages before understanding those differences could leave me sending more people through a confusing experience.

Trust is part of the first useful experience

There is another reason someone might hesitate even after understanding the product: they have to decide whether to put their information into it. A demonstration with sample data can reduce the effort needed to evaluate the workflow, but using the application for real asks for more trust.

For any task involving personal or financial information, I would want the product to explain what it stores, what happens to that information, and how a person can leave. Those explanations need to match the actual implementation. I cannot make a privacy or security promise simply because it would look reassuring on the landing page.

Support belongs in that decision too. A person should be able to find a way to report a problem and understand what help they can reasonably expect. As an independent builder, I need to be honest about that commitment. Offering personal onboarding is useful only if I leave enough time to follow through.

This is part of what makes a small MVP a serious product decision. I can defer optional features while still needing a dependable core workflow. If the application loses the work someone just entered, a smaller backlog does not make their experience acceptable. The scope has to include the behavior people rely on, and I need to check it before asking them to move a real task into the application.

Growing MRR asks more than whether someone signed up

The screenshot recommends charging from day one instead of offering free trials. There is a useful question behind that advice: will someone pay for the outcome? A payment is more direct evidence of willingness to pay than an encouraging comment on LinkedIn.

I would still make the trial decision around the product. If someone needs to use it with their own information or across several days to judge the benefit, a trial could help them decide. If the value can be demonstrated clearly before purchase, charging immediately may make sense. I would not dismiss every free user as unserious; their experience can reveal a problem that also affects paying users.

Monthly recurring revenue is an objective I care about. To make progress toward it, I need to understand what would justify an ongoing payment from the people I am trying to reach. Choosing a price or removing a free trial does not answer that question on its own.

The advice to price based on value is more useful to me than copying another application's subscription page. I would want to ask about the task a person is doing now: how they handle it, what is frustrating, and what a useful improvement would look like. Time saved, a recurring task made easier, or a mistake avoided could give the discussion a concrete basis. Those are possibilities to investigate, not benefits I can assign a monetary value to without talking to people.

Those conversations could happen through a DM, an email, or a short call, depending on what the person prefers. A focused question about what they tried to do would give me more to work with than asking whether they like the product. I would also want to hear from someone who created an account and then stopped, rather than only from people willing to praise it.

This is where retention belongs alongside the work of finding new users. If people try the product and do not return, reaching a larger audience leaves that question unresolved. I would want to understand repeated use before scaling the same acquisition attempt. For a recurring subscription, whether people keep finding a reason to use the product matters to the revenue goal too.

If a person leaves, an optional conversation could help explain what happened. I would make unsubscribing or cancelling straightforward, and respect a person who does not want to explain. An email opt-out might mean they want fewer messages; a product cancellation asks a different question. Either can be feedback, but neither gives me a reason to argue with their decision.

I also need to understand the expected frequency of the task. Someone may get value from a product every week or at a particular point in the month. Daily activity would be a poor way to judge that experience if daily use was never the goal. I would look for people returning when the need occurs and completing the task they came for.

Feedback from those conversations needs a decision attached to it. A request for another feature might reveal a missing step in the core workflow, or it might describe a different product. I would record what the person was trying to accomplish before putting the request into the backlog. That gives me a way to compare it with other needs instead of letting the most recent message determine the next epic.

I need to know where the attempt stops working

Once I start trying channels outside LinkedIn, a total sign-up count will leave too much unexplained. I want enough visibility to distinguish a message that people never saw from a product they tried and then abandoned.

A simple record could follow the path from first contact to continued use:

Step What I would try to learn
Someone encounters the product Which conversation, post, article, or recommendation brought them there?
They visit the page Can they understand the problem it addresses and the next action?
They create an account Where do they hesitate or leave during registration?
They complete the main task Do they get the outcome that made them try it?
They return when needed Does the product fit an ongoing need?
They begin or continue paying What makes the ongoing price worthwhile to them?

That main task needs a definition for each product before its completion becomes a useful signal. Opening a dashboard might only show that registration worked. The meaningful action should reflect what the person wanted to accomplish, and any measurement should collect only the information needed to understand that behavior.

With a small number of users, raw counts and conversations need to sit alongside any percentages. A few people leaving at one step would justify looking at it; it would not give me a reliable explanation of why everyone leaves. The channel context matters too. People arriving from my existing network may behave differently from people encountering the product for the first time.

This could make the next decision more specific. If people understand the offer but cannot finish the task, I have something to investigate in the product. If the people I reach do not recognize the problem, I need to examine the audience or message. Changing both at once would make it harder to understand what helped.

The costs behind the MRR goal

MRR also needs more detail than one rising total. Stripe's explanation of monthly recurring revenue separates growth from new subscriptions and existing customers increasing their subscriptions, and reductions from cancellations or downgrades. Those movements describe different situations that I would want to understand separately.

For example, new subscriptions could increase the total while existing subscribers leave. I would want to see both movements before deciding to repeat the acquisition effort. A larger total on its own would not explain whether the product is keeping the users it already reached.

Then I need to compare recurring revenue with the costs of providing the service. Hosting, payment processing, and support take resources. Where a product uses paid external services, their usage belongs in that calculation too. MRR measures recurring revenue; it does not show what remains after those costs.

The implementation workflow has costs as well, and the time spent helping users has to fit into the week. Even if AI makes an implementation task cheaper for me, I still need to maintain the behavior it introduces and answer questions about it. That is another reason to keep the scope of a growth experiment manageable.

A lifetime deal offered simply to produce early cash would deserve particular scrutiny. An ongoing service creates ongoing work, while a one-time payment has a different revenue shape from a recurring subscription. Before making that offer, I need to understand the support commitment it would create. This is a possible decision to examine; I am not reporting a pricing change to either product.

Ambition needs a reason to continue

The post also encourages builders to aim beyond their first revenue milestone. I like the challenge to think about what a product could become. At the same time, a larger MRR target needs some basis: who else could benefit, how I could reach them, and whether they would keep using it. Changing the number in a goal would leave my current acquisition problem untouched.

For Brainy and MoneyBrain, I want the next milestone to answer one of those questions while leaving room for a bigger ambition.

What I want to do with the next cycle of work

My next useful step would be to give one attempt at finding users the same attention I give an implementation task. Choose a specific audience and problem, make a small attempt to reach them, and leave time to follow up with anyone who tries the product.

A short note for each attempt could record the audience, the message, where I shared it, and what happened afterward. Including the effort spent, even if no money changed hands, would give me something to compare when deciding what to repeat.

For this purpose, focusing on one product at a time would make the follow-up easier to manage. Brainy and MoneyBrain can both remain part of my work, but trying a new audience and message for both simultaneously would divide that attention. AI gives me a way to move implementation forward; I still have to make room in the week to understand the people using the result.

I would set a review point before starting. With a limited budget, I need to consider the time spent as well as the money. Continuing an experiment should depend on what I learn from it; persistence alone would not tell me whether to repeat it, change it, or stop.

That connects two pieces of advice in the screenshot: stay in the game, and consider moving on when the product does not make money. If the goal is a business, revenue and costs need an honest review. Personal usefulness can be a separate reason to maintain it, but it does not establish commercial demand. I want to give a promising idea a fair test without treating every additional month of work as evidence that it will succeed.

I still value the workflow from the previous post. It helps me turn a product idea into software I can review. With Brainy and MoneyBrain, my immediate challenge is to take the next step beyond my LinkedIn circles and learn why someone unfamiliar with me would choose to use what I built.

AI assisted with drafting and editing this post and generating the cover image.

articles.title: Behind the scenes, two months later: How we ship Google Agent Skills like products
articles.description: In my previous post, I took you behind the scenes of Google Agent Skills, covering how the project...
articles.body_html:
In my previous post, I took you behind the scenes of Google Agent Skills, covering how the project started, how we maintain quality at scale, and how we handle governance. In this post, I'll share what we've built since then: the automated quality gates every change must pass, the AI review agent that inspects skill quality, and the lessons we learned along the way. You can adopt the same gates and review rules in your own skill repository.

Since my last post, the Google Agent Skills repository has passed 21,000 GitHub stars, up from 15,000. It now hosts over 170 skills from teams across Google, and we distribute them across multiple AI platforms.

Building agent skills for a single developer or a small project is straightforward. You write a SKILL.md file, define a few instructions, test it manually, and it works. At our scale, manual workflows stop being effective. Unvetted edits can introduce subtle bugs, and it becomes difficult to catch issues before they reach users.

The core philosophy: Ship skills like products

One key lesson from my previous post: a skill is a living product, not a one-off document. In practice, that means we ship every skill update like a product release.

It's tempting to treat a skill as documentation. But documentation explains concepts to a human reader, while a skill steers an AI agent's reasoning loop, tool selection, and execution path. A misplaced phrase in a skill can cause an agent to invoke invalid command flags, enter an infinite loop, or waste tokens.

That makes every instruction edit a behavioral change. You wouldn't ship a product update without testing it, and the same goes for a skill. This principle drives three core requirements:

  • Strict semantic versioning: Every behavioral change requires an explicit version bump.
  • Deterministic automated validation: Linters and validators check every proposed change before a human or AI reviewer sees it.
  • Mandatory evaluation evidence: Every change includes an evaluation report. It compares the skill against its previous version, or against an agent without the skill if the skill is new.

Automated conformance gates: The pull request pipeline

In my previous post, I briefly listed the checks every skill passes on check-in: linters, link checkers, and AI-assisted checklists. Here's what's inside them, plus two gates I haven't covered before: semantic versioning and evaluation suite validation.

When an author submits a change to our internal skills repository, an automated continuous integration and continuous delivery (CI/CD) pipeline triggers immediately. A skill must pass six automated gates and human approval before it's exported to GitHub:

  • Structural conformance: Directory layout, allowed files, taxonomy
  • Skill linters: Frontmatter, folder naming, Markdown rules
  • Semantic versioning: Version bump for every behavioral change
  • Evaluation suite: Valid eval suite and a fresh eval report
  • Link validation: Relative links are valid
  • AI review agent: Skill quality and design standards
  • Human approval: Final approval from a human reviewer (subject matter expert)

Structural conformance and skill linters

Our automated validation suite inspects every pull request for structural and syntactical correctness. Some of the rules include:

  • Folder name and metadata name must match
  • SKILL.md and description length limits are enforced
  • All required fields in the frontmatter metadata are present
  • Only a curated list of files and directories is allowed within a skill directory
  • All Markdown files follow formatting rules
  • The main README.md and the machine-readable index.json registry are up to date

Semantic versioning

Every skill declares a semantic version in its SKILL.md frontmatter metadata:

---
name: spanner-basics
metadata:
  version: "1.1.1"
  category: Databases
description: "..."
---

First, our automated checks verify that the version is a quoted string. YAML parses unquoted values such as 2.0 as numbers, which causes unexpected parsing errors in tools that expect a string.

Second, the validator checks the version transition itself. New skills must start at 1.0.0, and any change to an existing skill's instructions, scripts, or references requires a version bump or the pull request is blocked. Standard reset rules apply: bumping MAJOR (for example, 1.4.2 to 2.0.0) resets MINOR and PATCH to 0, and bumping MINOR (for example, 1.4.2 to 1.5.0) resets PATCH to 0.

Why enforce strict versioning if the agent only reads the Markdown instructions? The version number is for the developer and their package tooling, not for the model at runtime. Skills don't auto-update in the background, which means there's no network check or latency overhead each time an agent invokes a skill. Instead, explicit versions let developers compare their locally installed skills against the upstream catalog and decide when to pull changes — for example, by running npx skills update. This also supports workflows where teams want to lock a critical skill to a known-good version to guarantee reproducible agent behavior across their projects.

Evaluation suite validation

Our continuous evaluations (evals) compare agent performance with and without each skill. Those results are only as reliable as the evaluation suites behind them. If a suite contains broken file references or compound expectations, test results become noisy and untrustworthy.

Our validator parses each evaluation suite and the pull request description, then checks several strict invariants:

  • Resolution of file-based prompts: When a test prompt references a file (such as @file:test_prompt.txt), the validator confirms that the target file exists and isn't empty.
  • Atomic expectations: Each expectation must check exactly one criterion. The validator blocks compound expectations until authors split them. Lesson 2 later in this post shows why.
  • Duplicate detection: The validator flags duplicate test prompts and conflicting expectations within the same evaluation suite.
  • Mandatory evaluation report: Every pull request that modifies a skill must link to an evaluation report in its description.
  • Eval staleness check: Authors usually iterate on a pull request as reviewers leave feedback. The validator confirms that the linked report ran against the latest commit.

Link validation

Over 170 skills link to documentation for fast-evolving Google products, and those pages can move long after a skill passes review. Rather than waiting for users to report broken links, we validate links at two stages. Before merge, pull request checks verify all relative links, such as files in references/.

Then, every Monday, a GitHub Actions workflow runs lychee across all external links in the public repository and routes any broken links to skill owners for remediation.

AI review agent

Linters and schema validators catch syntactic errors, but they can't evaluate overall quality. They can't tell you if an instruction is confusing, if a reference guide is too verbose, or if a task should have been a bash script instead of a large language model (LLM) instruction.

To solve this, we integrated an AI review agent into our review pipeline. When a change affects a skill, the AI reviewer inspects it using a dedicated review skill. Yes, we use a skill to review skills.

Here are the core rules the AI reviewer evaluates. You can adopt these rules in your own skill development workflows.

1. Skill suitability and the deterministic trap

The first question our AI reviewer asks is simple: Does this task belong in an instruction?

We often see authors fall into the "deterministic trap." They write rigid, numbered sequences of command-line interface (CLI) commands directly into Markdown text.

LLMs are probabilistic engines. If an operation requires a strict sequence of commands where a variation can cause an error, embedding those commands in the instruction text invites hallucinations.

Our AI reviewer enforces a clear boundary between deterministic and probabilistic logic. Rigid CLI sequences, JSON parsers, and deployment steps must live in executable scripts under scripts/. Markdown instructions are reserved for tasks that require judgment, such as choosing an architecture, diagnosing error logs, or synthesizing code.

This rule complements the Model Context Protocol (MCP) guidance I shared last time: prefer remote MCP tools whenever possible. When you must fall back to CLI or API calls, wrap them in a script instead of spelling them out in the instructions.

2. The L1/L2/L3 modular architecture

Context windows are valuable. Loading a 2,000-line skill into an agent consumes context and degrades reasoning.

Our AI reviewer enforces a three-tier information hierarchy that follows the progressive disclosure model of Agent Skills:

  • Level 1 (Metadata): The YAML frontmatter (name, description). The agent uses this concise summary for discovery and routing.
  • Level 2 (Core instructions): The main SKILL.md file. The body must stay compact (under 500 lines). It provides workflow overviews, decision trees, and guardrails.
  • Level 3 (Reference docs): Detailed API references, schemas, and other reference tables live in a references/ directory.

Our AI reviewer enforces two distinct rules for Level 3: flat directory structure and single-hop indirection. Keeping references/ flat (no subdirectories) is a repository convention that discourages sprawling documentation trees and makes file discovery simpler. More importantly for runtime performance, the reviewer blocks chained references, where SKILL.md links to a reference file that links to yet another file. Each hop requires an extra tool call, adding latency and cost, and our evaluations showed that agents frequently stop before following a second level of chained references.

3. Non-interactive script design

When skills bundle helper scripts in scripts/, we expect agents to execute them directly in terminal sandboxes.

Our AI reviewer flags any script that blocks on interactive prompts. Every script must accept inputs through command-line flags or environment variables, provide --help documentation, and include a --dry-run or confirmation flag for destructive operations. Scripts also need to separate output cleanly, writing structured data (usually JSON) to standard output and actionable error messages to standard error.

Example AI review checklist snippet

The review skill also checks frontmatter for spec compliance and discovery, and turns the L1/L2/L3 architecture into concrete structure rules. Here's an excerpt from those criteria:

### Front Matter & Discovery

-   **Spec Compliance**: YAML front matter MUST strictly follow the Agent Skills
    Reference Specification (https://agentskills.io/specification). Use `>-`
    (folded strip-chomping) format for multi-line descriptions.
-   **Name Constraints**: The `name` field must be **64 characters or less**,
    correspond to the product name, use kebab-case (`[a-z0-9-]`), and avoid
    vague names (`helper`, `utils`, `tools`, `data`). The `name` field must
    match the directory name where it's located (i.e. `skills/cloud/gcloud`
    directory should contain a front matter with `name: gcloud`).
-   **Description Quality**: The `description` field must follow the
    [Description Guide](references/description_guide.md).

### Content Structure & Authoring Quality

-   **L1/L2/L3 Architecture**: Enforce modular structure. The main `SKILL.md`
    body must stay under 500 lines. Move deep domain reference material to
    `references/` (see [Skill Structure](references/skill_structure.md)).
-   **Flat References Directory**: `references/` must be a flat directory (one
    level deep, no nested subdirectories). References > 100 lines must include a
    Table of Contents with line hints (see
    [Skill Structure](references/skill_structure.md)).
-   **Avoid Deeply-Nested References**: Avoid deeply-nested references (e.g.,
    `SKILL.md` -> `references/guides.md` -> `assets/output.tmpl`). Keep
    reference structures shallow (one level of indirection from `SKILL.md`)
    because agents might not load such link targets fully.

Human approval

After passing all automated checks, every pull request must receive approval from a human reviewer. The reviewer is typically the skill's subject matter expert and, for new skills, a member of the Central Skills team.

Lessons learned from repository history

Six months of commit history and pull request discussions reveal several practical takeaways.

1. Scope CI checks carefully

Early in the project, we configured automated pull request checks with coarse directory globs.

One check required an approved bug tracking ticket on every change. Because the glob matched too broadly, engineers making a one-line typo fix were blocked for missing a tracking ticket. Meanwhile, newly added skills in deeper subdirectories went uninspected.

Takeaway: Match automated check rules to specific file operations, such as added versus modified files, and verify exact path depths. Treat minor edits to existing skills differently from new skills.

2. Atomic expectations

When we started writing evaluation suites, we saw authors write compound expectations, such as:

# Bad: Compound expectation
- "The agent must create a Cloud Storage bucket in us-central1, enable
  uniform bucket-level access, and apply lifecycle rules."

If the agent configured the region and lifecycle rules but missed the uniform access flag, the LLM-as-a-judge scorer returned inconsistent ratings.

Migrating to atomic expectations resolved this issue:

# Good: Atomic expectations
- "The agent specifies us-central1 for the bucket location."
- "The agent enables uniform bucket-level access on the created bucket."
- "The agent defines a lifecycle configuration rule deleting objects
  older than 30 days."

Takeaway: Check exactly one criterion per expectation. Atomic expectations make evaluation results clear, reliable, and debuggable.

3. Documentation drift happens fast

In a multi-contributor repository, documentation tables drift within days if maintained manually.

Takeaway: If you publish an index or catalog, never rely on contributors to update it manually. Instead, write a generator script and enforce it with a CI unit test. That's the origin of the README.md and index.json check in our linters. Our index.json even opens with a warning: "This file is generated. Do not edit it by hand."

4. Gate expensive LLM checks behind fast deterministic ones

Running full evaluation suites and an AI review agent on every change can get expensive fast, both in token usage and CI runtime — especially when authors push frequent small commits during review.

In our pipeline, fast deterministic checks run first. Structural conformance, skill linters, and semantic versioning act as blocking gates: if any of them fail, the pipeline stops immediately and won't trigger the AI reviewer or evaluation checks until those issues are fixed.

Takeaway: Stage your pipeline so cheap, deterministic checks block broken changes before LLM-powered gates run. When building a similar system, consider adding further cost guardrails, such as manual triggers for heavy checks (for example, a /run-evals pull request comment) or only triggering automatic re-runs when the diff exceeds a specific threshold.

Conclusion

Building a scalable Agent Skills repository requires more than good prompt engineering. It requires solid developer infrastructure:

  • Ship skills like products: version, validate, and evaluate every change.
  • Enforce semantic versioning and atomic expectations with automated CI gates.
  • Use an AI reviewer to catch design anti-patterns, such as the deterministic trap.
  • Check links before merge and on a weekly schedule.

Links and further reading

To get started with Google Agent Skills, check out:

  • Google Agent Skills repo: github.com/google/skills
  • Previous post: Behind the scenes: How we build, test, and scale Google Agent Skills
  • Launch announcement: Level Up Your Agents: Announcing Google's Official Skills Repository
  • Skills tutorial: Introduction: What Are Google Cloud Agent Skills?

What's next?

If you found this post helpful:

  • Share this post with your friends on social media.
  • Connect with me via LinkedIn, X, or Bluesky.

Thanks for reading!

articles.description: NVIDIA's GPU Is Closed Hardware With a Compiler Inside It. Here's What Reverse Engineering...
articles.body_html:
NVIDIA's GPU Is Closed Hardware With a Compiler Inside It. Here's What Reverse Engineering Actually Found.

NVIDIA documents PTX and keeps SASS, the machine code your kernels actually run as, undocumented. Everything below that line was learned the hard way, by timing hand-written instructions on real silicon. This covers what that work found, who did it, and which results I'd trust.

The Compiler Is Part of the Hardware

The best single paper here is Analyzing Modern NVIDIA GPU Cores from UPC Barcelona. Its method is simple. Write short sequences of hand-written SASS, wrap them in reads of the GPU clock counter, and use the elapsed cycles to confirm or refute a hypothesis. The authors used CuAssembler for this, the latest in a line of third-party assemblers that began with MaxAS.

The central finding is that modern NVIDIA hardware doesn't check most hazards itself. It relies on the compiler to encode dependencies in control bits on every instruction. Three mechanisms do the work:

  • Stall counter. For fixed-latency producers, the compiler sets a per-warp counter, and the hardware doesn't check RAW hazards for these instructions at all. A wrong value gives a wrong answer, not a stall.
  • Dependence counters. For variable-latency work like memory loads, each warp has six counters (SB0–SB5), each counting up to 63, with a 6-bit mask per instruction saying which to wait on. One counter can be released at register read (for WAR hazards) and another at write-back, which matters because source operands are often read hundreds of cycles before the result lands.
  • Reuse bit. The register file cache is software-managed through a per-operand reuse bit.

Two findings contradict what academic simulators assumed. There is no operand collector stage, since variable operand-fetch time would make fixed instruction latencies impossible. And the scheduler policy is "Compiler Guided Greedy Then Youngest", where the compiler's control bits steer a greedy-then-youngest warp selector.

The bank-conflict experiment is a good example of the method. Two back-to-back FFMAs took five cycles with odd source registers, six with one even, and seven with two even. That timing exposes a two-bank register file with one read port per bank.

The cost argument is where it gets interesting. Per the paper, the control-bit scheme needs 41 bits per warp, about 0.09% of an SM's register file, versus 5.32% for a scoreboard design with 63 consumers per entry. The authors' simulator model reached 13.98% mean error against an RTX A6000, 18.24 points better than Accel-Sim's baseline. They compare it to AMD, where a waitcnt instruction requires an explicit extra instruction rather than control bits.

Limits to keep in mind: the scheduler behavior is confirmed only for warps within one CTA, and the authors say they couldn't find a read policy matching every case. It's validated on Ampere and Turing, and the Hopper and Blackwell generations extend it with new tensor instructions.

Who Has Mapped the Rest

Mesa's NVK external hardware docs are the best index of public NVIDIA reverse engineering. They credit Kuter Dinel's nv_isa_solver with Hopper and Ada instruction encodings, point to nv-shader-tools for disassembly and fuzzing, and list envytools for Maxwell and earlier. They also describe tooling for dumping command sequences from the proprietary driver (envyhooks) and disassembling them (nv_push_dump).

That work feeds a real driver. Per the nouveau status page, NVK became a conformant Vulkan 1.4 implementation in December 2024, and was enabled for Blackwell and Kepler starting with Mesa 25.2.

The Driver Split Almost Nobody Mentions

The open-gpu-kernel-modules release changed what's reversible. NVIDIA started shipping open kernel modules with the R515 driver branch. Behind them sits a firmware boundary: the GPU System Processor is a RISC-V coprocessor, and NVIDIA's Resource Manager is split into a host CPU portion and a GSP portion. That has two consequences:

  1. Nouveau on RTX 40-series and later requires the GSP firmware blobs.
  2. There was no stable ABI for the GSP firmware at that point, so each driver version brought revised firmware. Treat the ABI point as dated, since it describes 2023.

The reverse-engineering target therefore moved. You can read the host side of the RM interface, but the firmware stays closed.

A Clean-Room CUDA Stack, With Footnotes

The most striking recent claim is a preprint on a clean-room toolchain for the GB10 (DGX Spark), with code in the CUDA++ repo. Its reported approach has three parts:

  • A roughly 900-line driver client written against the open kernel module's public headers, reproducing the object, memory, channel and submission sequence libcuda performs over ioctl.
  • Instruction encodings recovered from three sources: NVIDIA's compiler as an offline oracle on probe kernels, the open-source Mesa NAK compiler, and the chip itself, with arithmetic models fitted until output matched bit for bit.
  • Launches assembled in the order Mesa's NVK uses, with the launch descriptor (QMD) built directly.

The headline result: a 35-billion-parameter mixture-of-experts model served with zero CUDA libraries mapped in the process, its output identical to a host reference. Read the caveats before repeating that. It's a single-author Zenodo preprint, not peer reviewed, and the author says it was built by one engineer directing AI coding agents. The paper states its own boundaries: NVIDIA's open kernel module remains in the path, and GSP firmware stays NVIDIA's because the chip verifies its signature. So this is a replacement for the user-space stack, not for the whole trust chain.

Blackwell: Measured Versus Marketed

Two microbenchmark papers cover Blackwell, and they differ in how much to trust them. The GB203 study reports that low-precision mma.sync PTX instructions translate to new SASS opcodes (QMMA and OMMA) on Blackwell, where Hopper consistently uses HMMA.

The B200 study describes the architectural shift in more detail. Per the paper, Blackwell replaces warp-synchronous MMA with tcgen05.mma, a single-thread instruction, with operands from shared memory or a new Tensor Memory (TMEM). TMEM is 256 KB per SM, laid out as 128 lanes by 512 columns of 32-bit cells, managed in software through the tcgen05 instruction family. Its PTX-to-SASS table maps FP4 to OMMA and FP6/FP8 to QMMA, and FP64 is not supported by tcgen05.mma.

I'd verify its numbers before quoting them. The paper says it couldn't share code under double-blind review, uses hedged phrasing such as "consistent with a spatial array design" for its microarchitecture inferences, and says dual-die behavior across the NV-HBI link remains future work. A reasonable way to use it: take the instruction mappings and TMEM structure as leads, and re-measure any latency or throughput figure on your own hardware.

What Reverse Engineering Can't Tell You

It shows structure, not intent. Microbenchmarks recover latencies, port counts and policies, and they say nothing about why NVIDIA chose them. They also age fast, since each generation changes tensor instructions while the control-bit scheme carries forward. As a cross-check, the UPC authors note NVIDIA's own diagrams show significant changes limited mostly to tensor cores, ray tracing units and minor features.

The practical rule for this space: trust a claim only if it traces to a timing experiment, an open driver header, or a disassembly you can reproduce.

Follow for more coverage on MCP, agentic AI, and AI infrastructure.

articles.title: Your Agent's Config Is a Dependency With No Lockfile
articles.description: Your dependency policy is probably decent. Locked versions, hash verification, an SBOM if you're...
articles.body_html:
Your Agent's Config Is a Dependency With No Lockfile

Your dependency policy is probably decent. Locked versions, hash verification, an SBOM if you're serious, a review gate for new packages.

Meanwhile your coding agent imports instructions, skills, hooks, tool declarations, and subagents from public marketplaces and repositories. It runs all of it with your privileges, in your working directory, continuously. And none of it is in the lockfile, because the harness, as researchers now call this layer, has no lockfile.

What's Actually in the Harness

Inventory it sometime: the instruction files, the skills directory, the hooks that fire on events, the MCP server declarations, the subagent definitions. Each of these is code-shaped. Each was probably installed by copying a snippet from a README or a marketplace listing, sometimes written by a stranger, sometimes generated by another model.

We spent a decade teaching teams to treat npm installs as untrusted input. Then we built a new dependency layer, made it executable, made it ambient, and gave it a filename that sounds like configuration.

Someone Finally Measured It

In September 2026, researchers published the first systematic scan of the harness: 3,171 public GitHub repositories with assembled agent setups, 2,660 of them combining multiple component types, plus 511 published skill collections.

The results, and the method deserves respect: every finding was independently re-derived from the repository at its pinned commit, disagreements went to an adjudicator, and a second model session re-checked every counted pair.

16% of setups carry a security defect. The breakdown:

  • 9.8% install an MCP server with no version pinned. What you reviewed is not necessarily what runs.
  • 3.1% pre-approve arbitrary execution behind a scoped-looking grant. A permission like Bash(python:*) reads as contained and means anything Python can do, which is anything.
  • A third class ships inside skill collections: skills that pre-approve the shell for whoever installs them, arriving through marketplaces where a scan could theoretically see them.

The scary reading is the exploit chain. The accurate reading is quieter and worse: these are defects in ordinary setups, assembled by ordinary developers, following ordinary READMEs. Nobody got hacked in the study. Everybody got exposed.

Why This Is Not Like Packages

A dependency executes at build or test time, in a context you scaffolded. The harness runs as you, all the time, in the directory where your work and your secrets live. And its permissions read like configuration to a human scanning a PR diff, while functioning like a grant of execution to a machine reading them literally.

The scoped-looking grant is the perfect emblem: a permission string designed to feel surgical, meaning "run anything."

The Hygiene, Until the Ecosystem Grows Up

Pin everything. MCP server versions, skill sources, hook scripts. What changed since install is the first question an incident will ask.

Review config like dependency changes. The .claude directory and its cousins go through PRs, not direct commits. A config diff is a supply-chain diff.

Scan it. The study's instrument, corpus, and verdicts are released. Run it against your own setups before someone else's paper does.

Grant minimally, out loud. Enumerate what is pre-approved in your agent config, in a file a human reads monthly. The pre-approvals you forgot are the ones that get you.

💡 Pro-tip: the one-line audit: list every permission in your agent config that lets something execute without asking. If that list is longer than you remembered, you have found the article's point in your own repository.

What the Scan Misses

Scanning catches rule-decidable defects only. Intent cannot be scanned, and no lockfile standard exists for this layer yet, so this is manual discipline for now: pins, reviews, scans, minimal grants.

The harness is still worth it. So was npm. We just know how the first chapter of this story goes.

What's in your agent config directory that you didn't put there, and when did you last look?

References

  1. Scanning the Harness: An Empirical Study of Supply-Chain Defects in AI Coding-Agent Configurations (September 2026), instrument and data released: arxiv.org/abs/2609.07360
