articles.title: Why Tesseract Fails on Cursive Handwriting (And How We Built a Two-Tier Vision Pipeline in Node.js)
articles.description: When building Holder—a personal information vault and second brain for screenshots, links, and...
articles.body_html:
When building Holder—a personal information vault and second brain for screenshots, links, and documents—we ran into a classic computer vision bottleneck: handwritten lecture notes and cursive whiteboards.

If you've ever used classical OCR engines like Tesseract on handwritten notes, you know what happens:

Original handwriting: "A random process X(t) is said to be stationary if all its statistical properties..."
Tesseract output: "Sie xe esp Peo cep... fp yaudom Precen X(t) 2 Ad fe te sfefiono ~y i ike stafistieck Prepertioa..."

Here is why classical OCR fails on cursive handwriting, why sending every image to a multimodal AI model is a bad idea, and how we solved it with an automated two-tier pipeline.

1. Why Classical OCR Fails on Cursive

Classical OCR engines like Tesseract rely on Otsu binarization and character segmentation. They operate under the assumption that individual characters have distinct physical separation or predictable typographic spacing.

In cursive or student lecture notes:

Adjacent letters are connected by fluid, continuous strokes.
Letter heights, slants, and baselines continuously drift.
Letter boundaries do not exist in the traditional print sense.

Because Tesseract has no choice but to segment connected strokes, it chops words into random character fragments. It outputs strings of non-words with low confidence scores (often between 25% and 40%).

2. The Naive Fix (And Why It Fails in Production)

The obvious modern fix is: "Just send every image to a Vision LLM like GPT-4o, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, or Llama 3.2 Vision."

In production, this creates two major problems:

Upload Latency: Vision models take 3 to 8 seconds to process an image. If run synchronously on upload, the user sits staring at an "Uploading..." button unable to save.
Cost & Quota Burn: In a personal vault app, 80% of uploads are clean screenshots, tweets, terminal errors, or website bookmarks. Burning GPU cycles and API quotas on images that classical OCR can read in 800ms for $0 is wasteful.

3. The Architecture: Two-Tier Automated Fallback

To achieve sub-second saving, zero unnecessary API costs, and 100% handwriting transcription accuracy, we built a two-tier architecture:

[ User Uploads Image ] | v [ Save to Storage & Return UI Preview (< 400ms) ] --> User can save immediately | v (Background Queue) [ Tier 1: Fast Local OCR (Tesseract.js) ] | v [ Gibberish & Handwriting Heuristic Check ] | +---> [ Clean / High Confidence (> 80%) ] ----> Save Local OCR Output | +---> [ Gibberish / Handwriting Detected ] ---> [ Tier 2: Cloudflare Llama 3.2 11B Vision ] | v [ Extract Math & Cursive Text ] | v [ Live UI Update via Polling ]

4. The Gibberish Detection Heuristic

How does the server automatically know whether an image needs deep handwriting vision without human intervention?
We implemented a multi-factor lexical and statistical check in Node.js:

function shouldTriggerVisionHtr({ text, confidence, width, height }) {
  // 1. Tesseract confidence threshold (cursive handwriting typically scores < 65%)
  if (!confidence || confidence < 72) return true;
  // 2. Large canvas but sparse text (< 35 chars)
  if (width >= 300 && height >= 200 && text.length < 35) return true;
  const rawTokens = text.split(/\s+/).filter(Boolean);
  if (rawTokens.length >= 6) {
    const alphaTokens = rawTokens
      .map((t) => t.toLowerCase().replace(/[^a-z]/g, ''))
      .filter((t) => t.length >= 2);
    // 3. Valid English word ratio against a dictionary set
    if (alphaTokens.length >= 4) {
      const recognized = alphaTokens.filter((t) => COMMON_ENGLISH_WORDS.has(t)).length;
      const recognizedRatio = recognized / alphaTokens.length;
      // Low dictionary match ratio (< 42%) indicates garbled non-words
      if (recognizedRatio < 0.42 && confidence < 82) return true;
    }
    // 4. Fragmented stroke ratio (typical of chopped cursive: fy, fa, fp, te, fe)
    const shortTokens = rawTokens.filter((t) => t.replace(/[^a-zA-Z0-9]/g, '').length <= 2);
    const shortRatio = shortTokens.length / rawTokens.length;
    if (shortRatio > 0.35 && confidence < 82) return true;
    // 5. Unpronounceable consonant clusters (4+ consecutive consonants)
    const gibberishCount = rawTokens.filter(isGibberishToken).length;
    if (gibberishCount >= 2 && (gibberishCount / rawTokens.length) > 0.20 && confidence < 85) {
      return true;
    }
  }
  return false;
}

5. Tier 2: Serverless Vision Execution

When an image trips the gibberish check, it is dispatched to Cloudflare Workers AI running @cf/meta/llama-3.2-11b-vision-instruct on serverless edge GPUs.

Because multimodal LLMs process images through vision-language transformers, they do not merely segment characters—they understand linguistic semantics and domain context.

In our physics notes example:

Tesseract Word Accuracy: ~10% (confidence: 36%)
Llama 3.2 Vision Word Accuracy: 100% (transcribed formulas, strict sense stationary definitions, and bullet points perfectly)

6. Key Takeaways for Builders

Decouple Ingestion from AI Processing: Never block a user's upload flow on a heavy ML/LLM inference call. Store the file, render the preview, return HTTP 201, and process asynchronously.
Heuristic Routing Saves Budgets: Using classical OCR as a fast, zero-cost classifier allows you to reserve expensive vision models for the 20% of inputs that actually require them.
Lexical Analysis Over Confidence Alone: Confidence scores can be misleading (Tesseract can be 70% confident in a garbled word). Testing output tokens against a vocabulary dictionary provides a reliable signal for handwriting detection.

articles.title: skif: replacing sherif, syncpack and most of knip with one Rust binary
articles.description: I was working on restructuring a very large monorepo with disparate package managers and versions...
articles.body_html:
I was working on restructuring a very large monorepo with disparate package managers and versions into a single PNPM workspace. When I was finished I decided I am going to enforce certain conventions so it could not drift again without failing CI. I set this up, and found myself using several different tools - Sherif, Syncpack and Knip - to ensure that the repository doesn't drift again. This setup, while working, is rather clanky and also suffered from some issues - mainly performance, but also a few bugs.

I therefore decided I will build my own tool - forking Sherif as a baseline, and building on top of it while substantially rewriting and extending its capabilities. The result - still early - is skif: a Rust linter and enforcement tool for dependencies and monorepos.

skif replaces sherif and syncpack, and most of what knip does (the aim is to offer a full replacement for Knip in the future) in a single, ultra fast, binary.

npx skif-cli              # lint the workspace or package you are in
npx skif-cli --fix        # apply safe fixes
npx skif-cli migrate      # turn sherif, syncpack and knip config into a skif.toml

Where it came from

skif started as a fork of sherif, and the workspace and manifest rules are ported from it. The version
and catalog policies follow syncpack's model. The dead-code analysis follows knip's issue types.

It has since gone past the fork. It ports every sherif rule, adds new ones and fixes, and runs faster on every
target measured. On the syncpack side it enforces version, range, banned-dependency and catalog policy, and on a seeded workspace it reports the same 4,568 mismatched
instances syncpack does.

What it deliberately does not do is sync versions. skif is a linter: it tells you a policy is broken and
fails CI. Moving versions in step is left to specialized tools or the package manager's themselves.

What it checks

42 rules:

  • Manifests and workspace: empty dependency maps, types in dependencies, root private and packageManager, unsorted dependencies, workspace globs that match nothing, members without a package.json.
  • Version policy: mismatched versions, semver range policy, banned dependencies, catalogs (missing entries, unused entries, references that do not resolve), workspace: protocol, peer dependency compatibility.
  • Dead code: unused files, exports, types, enum members and dependencies; unlisted dependencies and binaries; unresolved imports; circular imports. Leveraging the OXC ecosystem for this.

It also adds some new rules, such as incompatible-peer-dependencies and workspace-protocol.

Skif lifts the idea of framework plugins - which allow it to understand different types of entrypoints (e.g. Next.JS, Vite, Storybook etc.). But unlike Knip, which loads these files, Skif doesn't actually load code - it only statically analyses it. This removes a potential surface for code execution, and is altogether much faster, although it does bring in the potential to some imprecision.

Supported package managers

Skif supports all major package managers - npm, pnpm, Yarn classic, Yarn Berry as well as Bun. It does not support Deno, although if there is a need it might in the future. It also supports Rush and Lerna workspaces.

Speed

Medians of 15 runs on a 4-vCPU Linux VM, pinned public repositories, dependencies installed:

Repository skif knip
create-t3-turbo 32 ms 2.0 s 61x
vue-core 62 ms 1.7 s 27x
tanstack-query 375 ms 4.5 s 12x
npm-cli 99 ms 968 ms 10x
babel 884 ms 7.2 s 8x

Manifest checks alone (--no-js) against sherif and syncpack:

Target skif sherif syncpack
create-t3-turbo 4.6 ms 36 ms 41 ms
babel 9.4 ms 37 ms 280 ms
2,000 generated packages 102 ms 130 ms 655 ms

sherif is already fast Rust, so the margin there is small: 1.3x at 2,000 packages. The real win is
knip, and not paying for three processes.

Reproduce with mise run bench:publish. The corpus is pinned in tools/bench/corpus.toml.

Accuracy

  • On a generated workspace with seeded manifest defects, skif finds exactly what sherif and syncpack find, defect for defect.
  • On a workspace with 33 seeded dead-code findings, placed next to live code reached through patterns that trip up static analysis (typeof import(), import.meta.glob, tsconfig paths, # subpath imports), skif scores 100% precision and 100% recall. knip 6.44.1 scores 77% precision and 100% recall.
  • On nine real repositories the agreement with knip is published per issue type. Unused exports match closely: 4,691 shared findings, 98% of skif's and 94% of knip's. Unused dependencies match less closely. Where it still differs from knip is listed rather than hidden.

Try it 

npx skif-cli migrate && npx skif-cli

Also brew install goldziher/tap/skif, scoop install skif, cargo install skif-cli. npm needs macOS or
Linux; on Windows use scoop or cargo.

It is 0.2.0 and younger than all three tools it builds on. If it reports something wrong on your
repo, open an issue with the repo and I will fix it.

Repository URL: https://github.com/Goldziher/skif

Docs URL: https://goldziher.github.io/skif/

articles.title: I wrote a VS Code extension because my settings.json kept getting shuffled
articles.description: Tidy Tint colors your VS Code window per workspace by editing settings.json as text, one key at a time, so your key order and comments survive.
articles.body_html:
I usually have three or four VS Code windows open at once. The API, the frontend, some side project, and whatever repo I opened "just to check something" two hours ago. They all look the same, so I'd regularly type into the wrong one.

The fix everybody knows is to give each workspace its own color. Blue title bar for the API, orange for the frontend, and so on. There are extensions for that and they work fine.

My problem was with what they did to .vscode/settings.json.

The diff that annoyed me

In a couple of my projects .vscode/settings.json is committed. I keep it organized by hand: related keys together, a comment here and there explaining why something is set. Every time I changed the color, the diff looked something like this:

   "workbench.colorCustomizations": {
-    // My own tweaks, grouped on purpose
     "editor.lineHighlightBackground": "#ffffff0d",
     "editorCursor.foreground": "#ffcc00",
-    // Workspace tint
-    "statusBar.background": "#2f6fd6",
+    "terminal.background": "#1b1b1f",
+    "statusBar.background": "#2e8b57",
     "statusBar.foreground": "#e7e7e7",
-    "statusBarItem.hoverBackground": "#447dda",
-    "terminal.background": "#1b1b1f"
+    "statusBarItem.hoverBackground": "#439768"
   }

Two values changed. The diff touches eight lines, both comments are gone, and terminal.background, which I never touched, jumped to the middle of the block.

It's not a bug in those extensions, really. It's how the VS Code API works. When you call

workspace.getConfiguration().update('workbench.colorCustomizations', newObject)

you're handing VS Code a brand new object, and it writes that object in place of the old one. Whatever order the keys have in newObject is the order you get in the file, and comments inside it are simply dropped because a JS object has nowhere to keep them.

So I wrote my own extension, Tidy Tint. It does the same job (color the activity bar, title bar and status bar per workspace) but it never calls update() for the colors. It edits the file as text.

Editing JSON as text without going crazy

Doing string surgery on JSON by hand sounds like a terrible idea, and it is. Luckily VS Code itself solves this problem with jsonc-parser, the same library it uses to read your settings. It understands comments and trailing commas, and it has a modify() function that, instead of returning a new document, returns a list of edits: "at offset X, replace N characters with this string".

That's exactly what I wanted. The rules I ended up with are:

  • if a key already exists, only its value changes, in place;
  • if it's new, it goes at the end of its object;
  • removing colors deletes only the keys Tidy Tint wrote, with their comma and their line;
  • nothing else in the file is touched.

The first version was basically applyEdits(text, modify(text, path, value, { formattingOptions })) in a loop, and it almost worked. The catch is that when you pass formatting options, jsonc-parser sometimes reformats the lines around the edit too. Not much, but enough to show up in the diff, which was the whole thing I was trying to avoid.

The workaround was to ask for the edits without formatting and then format only the text I just inserted:

function applyMinimal(text: string, edits: Edit[], options: FormattingOptions): string {
  for (const e of [...edits].sort((a, b) => b.offset - a.offset)) {
    text = text.slice(0, e.offset) + e.content + text.slice(e.offset + e.length);
    if (e.content.length > 0) {
      text = applyEdits(text, format(text, { offset: e.offset, length: e.content.length }, options));
    }
  }
  return text;
}

The edits are applied from the end of the file backwards so earlier offsets stay valid. The formatting options aren't hardcoded either: the extension looks at the file first and copies whatever it finds (tabs or spaces, indent width, \n or \r\n). If your file uses tabs and CRLF, so do the new lines.

Deleting a key is the annoying part

Adding and changing values was the easy half. Removing them cleanly took more fiddling than I expected, because of commas.

If the key is in the middle of the object, you delete from the start of its line to the start of the next key. If it's the last one, you have to eat the comma of the previous key instead, otherwise you're left with a trailing comma (valid in JSONC, but ugly and not what was there before). And if it's the only key, the object just becomes {}.

if (siblings.length === 1) {
  // Only property: the object becomes "{}".
  start = obj.offset + 1;
  end = obj.offset + obj.length - 1;
} else if (i < siblings.length - 1) {
  // Another one follows: delete from this property to the start of the next.
  start = lineStartIfOnlyIndent(text, prop.offset);
  end = lineStartIfOnlyIndent(text, siblings[i + 1].offset);
} else {
  // It's the last one: delete from the end of the previous one (including its comma).
  const prev = siblings[i - 1];
  start = prev.offset + prev.length;
  end = prop.offset + prop.length;
}

When you run "Remove Colors" and workbench.colorCustomizations ends up empty, the extension removes that key too, so you don't keep a lonely {} hanging around. If you had your own keys in there (like my cursor color or the terminal background) they stay exactly where they were.

Writing the file without breaking undo

The last detail: once I have the new text, I don't write it to disk with fs. I apply it with a WorkspaceEdit and then save the document. Two reasons. If you have settings.json open with unsaved changes, writing behind VS Code's back is asking for trouble. And with a WorkspaceEdit the change goes into the editor's history, so Ctrl+Z (Cmd+Z on Mac) undoes a color change like any other edit.

The colors

This part is less interesting but I'll mention it. You pick one base color and the extension derives the rest: foreground is light or dark depending on the base's luminance (the WCAG formula), inactive title bar is the same color with some transparency, the badge on the activity bar uses the hue rotated 150° so it stands out, and the hover color on the status bar is slightly lighter or darker. There are 13 keys in total, and those 13 are the only ones Tidy Tint will ever write or delete.

The random color isn't fully random either. It picks a random hue but keeps saturation and lightness in a range that doesn't give you neon green or a gray that looks like nothing changed.

Tests

Since the whole point of the extension is "don't mess up my file", the JSON editing code is tested with Node's built-in test runner, no extra framework. The tests are boring in a good way: take a settings file with comments and keys in a weird order, change the color twice, and check that the order of keys is identical and the comments are still there. Remove colors and check that only Tidy Tint's keys disappeared.

Using it

Install Tidy Tint from the Marketplace and open the command palette:

  • Tidy Tint: Change Color lets you pick from a list of favorites, type a hex value, or go random
  • Tidy Tint: Random Color if you don't care
  • Tidy Tint: Remove Colors to undo everything

You can turn off each bar separately (tidyTint.affectActivityBar, tidyTint.affectTitleBar, tidyTint.affectStatusBar) and change the favorites list in tidyTint.favoriteColors.

In a multi-root workspace the colors go in the .code-workspace file, so you need to save the workspace first.

One honest limitation: Tidy Tint only controls what it writes. If another extension or the Settings UI later rewrites workbench.colorCustomizations as a whole object, the order will change again. I can't do anything about that.

That's it

It's a small extension, around 350 lines of TypeScript, and it solves a problem that maybe only bothers people who read their own diffs too carefully. If you're one of them, give it a try.

The code is MIT and lives on GitHub: cbsumastre/tidy-tint. Issues and PRs are welcome, and if you find a settings file that it mangles, I'd really like to see it.

articles.title: POV: You Asked Your Coding Agent to Fix a Null Reference for the Third Time Today
articles.description: POV: You are staring at your screen while Claude Code rewrites the same async function four times...
articles.body_html:
POV: You are staring at your screen while Claude Code rewrites the same async function four times because TypeScript allowed undefined to sneak into a database response.

You watch the agent guess. It adds optional chaining. It adds a bang operator. It imports a type guard. None of it stops the crash when production hits an unexpected payload.

Coding agents run on a simple loop. They write, they run, they read the error, they fix. But if the language they write in relies on nulls and hidden exceptions, the loop gets stuck on guesswork.

I am Jake Burwick, a high school student, and I built Vow to fix this loop. Vow is an open source programming language under the MIT license built specifically for AI agents to write. The source code is public at github.com/JakeBurwick/vow.

Vow has no nulls and no exceptions. Every failure is a value. Functions return Result values that must be handled with match or the ? operator.

fn parsePrice(text) {
  let n = num(text)?
  if n < 0 { return err("can't be negative") }
  return ok(n)
}

When an agent hits a bug in Vow, it does not have to guess what went wrong. Every Vow error says what is wrong, where, and the likely fix. Errors are written as repair instructions an agent can act on without a human.

x TypeError: can't add a num and a str
-> line 6, col 10
6 | return "Total: " + sum
           ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
Likely fix: convert the number to text
first: str(sum)

Security is handled at the function level. Every function declares whether it can touch the network, files or environment using uses net, uses fs, or uses env. Before a single line executes, you can catch unauthorized access attempts.

$ vow --sandbox --allow fs=./data app.vow
x SandboxError: needs capabilities
  the sandbox does not grant
  env: fn leak declares 'uses env'
Nothing was run.

The command vow --sandbox checks capabilities before anything runs and refuses a program that reaches beyond what you allow.

Under the hood, Vow compiles to JavaScript. Recursive fib(32) runs in 0.09 s, against 0.14 s for Python, measured on October 7, 2026.

In tests conducted in October 2026 with Claude Haiku 4.5, code that agents finish passes fresh hidden tests at 99.5% for Vow and 99.3% for TypeScript. On three brand-new hard tasks, Vow had one failed submission in nine runs and TypeScript had zero, showing the two perform evenly on a small sample. In November 2026 tests, Claude Sonnet 5.5 and Opus 5.5 solved every run in both Vow and TypeScript, with Vow recording one failed submission in eighteen runs and TypeScript zero.

You can install it globally with npm:

npm install -g github:JakeBurwick/vow

If you use Claude Code, you can add the MCP server so the agent gets vow_guide, vow_check, and vow_run tools directly:

claude mcp add vow -- vow-mcp

To start using it with Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, or any coding agent, you paste a one-paragraph prompt from the site into your agent, which points it right at the guide. The site also includes an llms.txt and an AGENTS.md file that you can drop straight into a project so any coding agent picks up Vow immediately.

Head over to https://vow-lang.vercel.app to check out the playground, tutorial, docs, and the Errors page that puts five bugs side by side in Vow, TypeScript, and Python.

articles.title: Introducing Vectro: SQL and dataframes on every core, in JavaScript
articles.description: Vectro is an analytics engine that runs inside JavaScript apps instead of next to them. This post...
articles.body_html:
Vectro is an analytics engine that runs inside JavaScript apps instead of next to them. This post covers what it is, how fast it is, and where it isn't fast yet. Everything here can be checked: the benchmark scripts are in the repo, and there's a page that races it against DuckDB-WASM and Arquero in your browser.

Most JavaScript apps that need to add up, group or search a lot of data send it somewhere else first: a database, a warehouse, a Python service. Vectro does that work where the data already is, inside your Node server or your user's browser tab.

import { Engine, sql } from 'vectrojs';

const engine = new Engine();               // one worker per core
const orders = engine.readCSV('orders.csv');

sql(`SELECT region, COUNT(*) AS orders, SUM(price * qty) AS revenue
     FROM orders GROUP BY region ORDER BY revenue DESC`, { orders }).toRows();

What it is

Vectro keeps your data in columns in WebAssembly memory. When a query first runs, it is compiled into a SIMD WebAssembly loop, and every core runs that loop over its own share of the rows. There is no native addon to build and no dependency to install: it is JavaScript that writes its own WebAssembly.

  • SQL and a dataframe API. Joins (including outer joins), subqueries, CTEs, window functions, percentiles, text and date functions; or filter, groupBy and join from JavaScript.
  • Files bigger than memory. A .vectro dataset is read one chunk at a time, and every block of rows keeps its smallest and largest values, so a query skips what it doesn't need.
  • Everywhere JavaScript runs. Node 20 and later, browsers (Chrome, Safari and Firefox are checked on every change) and edge runtimes such as Cloudflare Workers.
  • Your BI tools. vectro serve speaks the PostgreSQL protocol, HTTP, OData and Arrow Flight SQL, so Power BI, Tableau, Metabase and Grafana can read your tables.

How fast

We compare against DuckDB because it is the best embedded analytics engine we know, and beating it on its own turf is the bar we set. On the same machine, with the same SQL and the same answers:

  • 20 of 20 SQL benchmark queries over 10 million rows were faster in Vectro, from 1.3 to 6.0 times.
  • Over a billion rows on disk, Vectro was level or faster on 7 of 8 queries and used 0.37 GB of memory where DuckDB used 6.9 GB. The top 10 rows by price took 11 ms against 843 ms, because Vectro skipped every block that couldn't hold a winning row.
  • DuckDB is still faster at a join over a file with a GROUP BY on the joined table's columns (1.4 times at a billion rows, 1.5 at 100 million), and at 100 million rows on one filter (1.1 times) and a lookup that reads a single chunk (3 ms against 1).

Every number, the scripts that produced it and the machine it ran on are on the benchmarks page. Or skip our numbers and race them in your own browser: Vectro, DuckDB-WASM and Arquero get the same rows and the same 13 questions, and every answer is checked.

Try it 

npm install vectrojs

Then the quick start takes about a minute. The source is on GitHub, under the MIT license.

Vectro isn't 1.0 yet (the changelog has the current version): the dataset file format may still change before then, and the streaming API is a prototype. If something is slow, wrong or missing, please open an issue, or write to info@vectrojs.dev.
